import Mathlib
/-! QED-M014: Two-frequency localization
For the lattice Schrödinger operator on ℤ with potential λ(cos 2π(n√2+θ₁) + cos 2π(n√3+θ₂)), prove that for all large λ and almost every phase θ the operator has pure point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions, for this specific frequency vector.
Informal statement: For $\lambda>0$ and $\theta\in\mathbb T^2$ let $(H_{\lambda,\theta}\psi)(n)=\psi(n+1)+\psi(n-1)+\lambda\big(\cos2\pi(n\sqrt2+\theta_1)+\cos2\pi(n\sqrt3+\theta_2)\big)\psi(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$. Prove there is $\lambda_0$ such that for all $\lambda\ge\lambda_0$ and Lebesgue-a.e. $\theta$, $H_{\lambda,\theta}$ has pure point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions (Anderson localization).
Formalization notes: Anderson localization (pure point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions) is encoded as the existence of a real orthonormal basis of ℓ²(ℤ) consisting of exponentially decaying eigenfunctions; for a bounded self-adjoint operator, pure point spectrum is equivalent to the eigenvectors being complete. Real eigenfunctions suffice since H is a real symmetric operator. Any ONB of ℓ²(ℤ) is countably infinite, so ℕ-indexing loses nothing. Orthonormality uses tsum, legitimate because exponential decay makes the products summable; completeness is Parseval's identity. θ ranges over ℝ² with Lebesgue measure; the potential is ℤ²-periodic in θ, so a.e. on ℝ² is the same as a.e. on the torus. Proving ¬Claim means: for arbitrarily large λ a positive-measure set of phases fails localization.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM014

/-- The quasi-periodic potential `λ (cos 2π(n√2 + θ₁) + cos 2π(n√3 + θ₂))`. -/
noncomputable def pot (lam : ℝ) (θ : ℝ × ℝ) (n : ℤ) : ℝ :=
  lam * (Real.cos (2 * Real.pi * ((n : ℝ) * Real.sqrt 2 + θ.1)) +
    Real.cos (2 * Real.pi * ((n : ℝ) * Real.sqrt 3 + θ.2)))

/-- `ψ` solves `H_{λ,θ} ψ = E ψ` pointwise. -/
def IsEigenfunction (lam : ℝ) (θ : ℝ × ℝ) (E : ℝ) (ψ : ℤ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℤ, ψ (n + 1) + ψ (n - 1) + pot lam θ n * ψ n = E * ψ n

/-- `ψ` decays exponentially. -/
def ExpDecaying (ψ : ℤ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ C c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ n : ℤ, |ψ n| ≤ C * Real.exp (-(c * |(n : ℝ)|))

/-- Anderson localization: `ℓ²(ℤ)` has an orthonormal basis `(ψ k)` of exponentially decaying
eigenfunctions of `H_{λ,θ}` (orthonormality plus Parseval's identity for every `ℓ²` vector). -/
def AndersonLocalized (lam : ℝ) (θ : ℝ × ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (ψ : ℕ → ℤ → ℝ) (E : ℕ → ℝ),
    (∀ k : ℕ, IsEigenfunction lam θ (E k) (ψ k) ∧ ExpDecaying (ψ k)) ∧
    (∀ k j : ℕ, ∑' n : ℤ, ψ k n * ψ j n = if k = j then (1 : ℝ) else 0) ∧
    (∀ φ : ℤ → ℝ, Summable (fun n : ℤ => φ n ^ 2) →
      HasSum (fun k : ℕ => (∑' n : ℤ, φ n * ψ k n) ^ 2) (∑' n : ℤ, φ n ^ 2))

/-- Large-coupling Anderson localization for a.e. phase, at the fixed frequency vector `(√2, √3)`. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ lam₀ : ℝ, ∀ lam : ℝ, lam₀ ≤ lam →
    ∀ᶠ θ in MeasureTheory.ae (MeasureTheory.volume : MeasureTheory.Measure (ℝ × ℝ)),
      AndersonLocalized lam θ

end OpenProblems.QEDM014
prov_reason: Fixed-frequency large-coupling localization for multi-frequency quasi-periodic operators is a recognised open problem (stated as unknown in arXiv:2603.07180); this is an explicit instance.

title: Wind-driven fire confinement threshold
credit: A. Bressan, Differential inclusions and the control of forest fires, J. Differential Equations 2007 (non-isotropic Thm 5)
results: sigma*(a,b) >= Lambda*(a-b), Lambda ~ 1.62621 (isotropic lower bound, arXiv 2610.36919, Thm 4.1). Proof: F contains the disc of radius a-b. Bressan's comparison lemma moves blocking from F to that disc, and rescaling time reduces to unit speed. sigma*(a,b) <= 2 max_{theta in [0,pi]} (a+b cos theta) sin theta (Bressan, Thm 5, non-isotropic case; applies because rho is even and nonincreasing on [0,pi]). This equals 2a at b=0 and tends to (3 sqrt3/2) a as b->a.
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.36919 (2026 preprint): isotropic lower bound Lambda ~ 1.6262 (Thm 4.1), used for the lower bound recorded in the notes.
plain: A fire spreads from a point, faster downwind: speed a + b cos(theta) in direction theta (0<=b<a). Firefighters build a barrier at speed sigma. Let sigma*(a,b) be the smallest speed that can confine the fire. Known: 1.626(a-b) <= sigma* <= 2 max (a+b cos theta) sin theta. Improve either bound, especially in the strong-wind limit b/a -> 1, where the lower bound tends to 0 but the upper bound stays near 2.6a.
math: With F_b = conv{r e^{i theta}: 0<=r<=1+b cos theta}, R_0 the open unit disc and Bressan-admissible barriers, prove that for some fixed b in (0,1) the fire can be confined with some sigma < 2 max_theta (1+b cos theta) sin theta, i.e. Bressan's anisotropic upper bound is not sharp.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M015: Wind-driven fire confinement threshold
A fire spreads from a bounded region with speed 1 + b cos θ in direction θ (0 ≤ b < 1, wind along the
positive x-axis); firefighters build barriers at speed σ (total length ≤ σt at time t). Bressan's
non-isotropic construction confines the fire whenever σ > U(b) := 2 max_θ (1 + b cos θ) sin θ.
Can one do strictly better for some wind strength?
Informal statement: (corrected) With F_b = conv{r e^{iθ} : 0 ≤ r ≤ 1 + b cos θ}, R₀ the open unit disc
and Bressan-admissible barriers (rectifiable, increasing, H¹(γ(t)) ≤ σt), show that for some fixed
b ∈ (0,1) some σ < 2 max_θ (1 + b cos θ) sin θ confines the fire (i.e. Bressan's upper bound is not
sharp for some fixed wind ratio). The original target "liminf_{b→a} σ*(a,b)/a > 0" is trivially true:
conv F contains the disc of radius ρ = min_u h_F(u) about 0, which equals a²/(4b) for b ≥ a/2, so
the comparison argument already gives σ* ≥ Λ·a²/(4b) → Λa/4 > 0.
Formalization notes: Scaling a = 1 loses nothing (σ*(a,b) = aσ*(1,b/a)). The plane is ℂ (Euclidean
metric, so `hausdorffMeasure 1` is length). R₀ is the open unit disc (with R₀ = {0} a single point
barrier at the origin would trivially block everything; the threshold does not depend on the bounded
open R₀). A barrier strategy γ is admissible at speed σ if it is increasing in t, each γ(t) is empty
or a countable union of Lipschitz images of [0,1] (Bressan's rectifiability condition), and
H¹(γ(t)) ≤ σt. Burned points at time t are x(t) for Lipschitz paths with |x(0)| < 1, ẋ(s) ∈ F_b
a.e. on [0,t] (Lipschitz paths are a.e. differentiable; any absolutely continuous path with
ẋ ∈ F_b is Lipschitz), and x(s) ∉ γ(s) for s ∈ [0,t]. Confinement: all burned points stay in a fixed
ball. Known: Λ·ρ(b) ≤ σ*(1,b) ≤ U(b), Λ ≈ 1.6262 (isotropic lower bound).
Proving `Claim` = exhibiting b ∈ (0,1) and a confining strategy of speed σ < U(b).
Proving `¬Claim` = Bressan's anisotropic construction is optimal for every b ∈ (0,1).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM015
noncomputable section

/-- Convexified spreading set for wind strength `b` (unit base speed). -/
def Fset (b : ℝ) : Set ℂ :=
  convexHull ℝ {z : ℂ | ∃ r θ : ℝ, 0 ≤ r ∧ r ≤ 1 + b * Real.cos θ ∧
    z = (r : ℂ) * Complex.exp ((θ : ℂ) * Complex.I)}

/-- Bressan-admissible barrier strategy of construction speed `σ`. -/
def Admissible (σ : ℝ) (γ : ℝ → Set ℂ) : Prop :=
  (∀ s t : ℝ, 0 ≤ s → s ≤ t → γ s ⊆ γ t) ∧
  (∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure (1 : ℝ) (γ t) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (σ * t)) ∧
  (∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → γ t = ∅ ∨
    ∃ c : ℕ → ℝ → ℂ, (∀ m : ℕ, ∃ K : NNReal, LipschitzWith K (c m)) ∧
      γ t = ⋃ m : ℕ, c m '' Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1)

/-- `z` is burned at time `t` (reached by an admissible fire path avoiding the barrier). -/
def Burned (b : ℝ) (γ : ℝ → Set ℂ) (t : ℝ) (z : ℂ) : Prop :=
  ∃ x : ℝ → ℂ, (∃ K : NNReal, LipschitzWith K x) ∧ ‖x 0‖ < 1 ∧ x t = z ∧
    (∀ᵐ s ∂MeasureTheory.volume, s ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) t → ∀ v : ℂ, HasDerivAt x v s → v ∈ Fset b) ∧
    ∀ s ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) t, x s ∉ γ s

/-- Speed `σ` suffices to confine the fire with wind `b`. -/
def Confines (b σ : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ γ : ℝ → Set ℂ, Admissible σ γ ∧ ∃ M : ℝ, ∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → ∀ z : ℂ, Burned b γ t z → ‖z‖ ≤ M

/-- Bressan's upper bound `2 max_θ (1 + b cos θ) sin θ`. -/
noncomputable def U (b : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  2 * sSup (Set.range fun θ : ℝ => (1 + b * Real.cos θ) * Real.sin θ)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ b : ℝ, 0 < b ∧ b < 1 ∧ ∃ σ : ℝ, σ < U b ∧ Confines b σ

end

end OpenProblems.QEDM015
M_fix_reason: The original main target liminf_{b->a} sigma*(a,b)/a > 0 is trivially true. Since F is convexified, conv F contains the disc of radius rho = min_u h_F(u) about 0, and rho = a^2/(4b) for b >= a/2 (at b=a, rho = a/4). The same comparison argument that gives Lambda(a-b) then gives sigma* >= Lambda a^2/(4b) -> Lambda a/4 > 0. Also R_0 = {0} is degenerate, because a single point barrier at the origin blocks everything; it was replaced by the unit disc.
prov_reason: This is an anisotropic (wind-driven) version of Bressan's fire confinement problem; the bounds were derived by QED.

title: Additive excess for sorting pattern-avoiding sequences
credit: Fredman 1976 (sorting with partial information); Opler, arXiv:2409.07868 (ESA 2025), sorting pattern-avoiding permutations
results: delta_tau >= 0: information-theoretic bound C_tau(n) >= log2|Av_n(tau)| (trivial). delta_tau <= 2: Fredman (1976), any set G of permutations can be sorted with log2|G| + 2n comparisons. Opler (arXiv 2409.07868) gives O((log c_tau +1)n), optimal only up to a constant factor. delta_tau = 0 is known for tau of length 3 in the 132-class (stack sorting, <=2n vs log2 C_n = 2n - O(log n)).
plain: Sorting an array promised to avoid a fixed pattern needs at least log2 of the number of allowed orders comparisons, and Fredman's theorem says 2n more always suffice. How many extra comparisons per element are really needed? Show that fewer than 2n extra suffice for 1324-avoiding inputs, or show that a linear excess is necessary for some pattern.
math: For a permutation τ let C_τ(n) be the minimum worst-case number of comparisons of a decision tree (knowing τ) that sorts a_1,…,a_n under the promise that their order pattern lies in Av_n(τ), and δ_τ = limsup_n (C_τ(n) − log_2|Av_n(τ)|)/n ∈ [0,2]. Prove or disprove: δ_τ = 0 for every permutation τ.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M016: Additive excess for sorting pattern-avoiding sequences
Sorting an input promised to avoid a fixed pattern τ needs at least log2 |Av_n(τ)| comparisons,
and Fredman's theorem gives log2 |Av_n(τ)| + 2n. Is the excess always o(n)?
Informal statement: For a permutation τ let C_τ(n) be the minimum worst-case number of comparisons of a decision tree (knowing τ) that sorts a_1,…,a_n under the promise that their order pattern lies in Av_n(τ), and δ_τ = limsup_n (C_τ(n) − log_2|Av_n(τ)|)/n ∈ [0,2]. Prove or disprove: δ_τ = 0 for every permutation τ.
Formalization notes: An input order is a permutation σ of Fin n, where σ i is the rank of a_i;
the comparison "a_i < a_j?" is σ i < σ j. A comparison tree (`CompTree n`) has leaves labelled by
permutations and internal nodes labelled by a pair (i, j); `run t σ` follows the comparisons and
returns the leaf label. A tree sorts the class if `run t σ = σ` for every σ avoiding τ. Depth is
the worst-case number of comparisons. σ contains τ (of length k) if some strictly increasing
e : Fin k → Fin n has σ(e a) < σ(e b) ↔ τ a < τ b. δ_τ = 0 is encoded as: for every ε > 0 and
all large n there is a sorting tree of depth <= log2 |Av_n(τ)| + εn (δ_τ >= 0 is automatic).
For patterns of length <= 2 the statement is trivial (|Av_n| <= 1). Proving Claim answers yes
for all τ; proving ¬Claim exhibits a τ with δ_τ > 0. The weaker target δ_1324 < 2 from the
original is not encoded. Known: 0 <= δ_τ <= 2 (Fredman 1976).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM016

/-- Comparison decision trees on n keys. -/
inductive CompTree (n : ℕ) where
  | leaf : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) → CompTree n
  | node : Fin n → Fin n → CompTree n → CompTree n → CompTree n

/-- Run a comparison tree on the input whose order is `σ` (σ i = rank of the i-th key).
At `node i j l r` go left iff key i is smaller than key j. -/
def CompTree.run {n : ℕ} : CompTree n → Equiv.Perm (Fin n) → Equiv.Perm (Fin n)
  | CompTree.leaf π, _ => π
  | CompTree.node i j l r, σ => if σ i < σ j then CompTree.run l σ else CompTree.run r σ

/-- Worst-case number of comparisons. -/
def CompTree.depth {n : ℕ} : CompTree n → ℕ
  | CompTree.leaf _ => 0
  | CompTree.node _ _ l r => max (CompTree.depth l) (CompTree.depth r) + 1

/-- `σ` contains the pattern `τ`. -/
def Contains {k n : ℕ} (τ : Equiv.Perm (Fin k)) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : Fin k → Fin n, StrictMono e ∧ ∀ a b : Fin k, (σ (e a) < σ (e b) ↔ τ a < τ b)

/-- |Av_n(τ)|. -/
noncomputable def avCount {k : ℕ} (τ : Equiv.Perm (Fin k)) (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card {σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) // ¬ Contains τ σ}

/-- `t` sorts every input whose order pattern avoids `τ`. -/
def SortsAv {k n : ℕ} (τ : Equiv.Perm (Fin k)) (t : CompTree n) : Prop :=
  ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), ¬ Contains τ σ → CompTree.run t σ = σ

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ (k : ℕ) (τ : Equiv.Perm (Fin k)) (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε →
    ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n →
      ∃ t : CompTree n, SortsAv τ t ∧
        (CompTree.depth t : ℝ) ≤ Real.logb 2 (avCount τ n : ℝ) + ε * (n : ℝ)

end OpenProblems.QEDM016
M_fix_reason: M is 'improve either bound for some τ, in particular δ_1324 < 2, or find τ with δ_τ > 0; is δ_τ = 0 for all τ?'. Several targets of different strength; formalized the final, sharpest yes/no question 'δ_τ = 0 for every τ'.
prov_reason: Refines Fredman's generic log2|G|+2n bound and Opler's O(n)-excess sorting of pattern classes into the question of the exact additive excess constant; no source poses δ_τ.

title: Blank jigsaw with few edge shapes
credit: Mossel & Ross (shotgun assembly); Bordenave, Feige, Mossel 2016, arXiv:1605.03086; Nenadov, Pfister, Steger 2017, arXiv:1701.04813
plain: A jigsaw with no picture can only be solved from the shapes of its pieces. Each internal edge is one of k shapes (a tab that fits only its own matching blank), and pieces may be turned. How small can k be if some n×n blank jigsaw still goes together in exactly one way? Counting shows k must be at least about √n, and random puzzles need about n.
math: An $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types is a map assigning to each internal edge of the $n\times n$ grid a type in $[k]$ and an orientation (which side carries the tab); border edges are flat. Its pieces are the $n^2$ unit squares, each regarded as a distinct physical object carrying its four (type, tab/blank) labels up to rotation. An assembly is a placement of all pieces bijectively on the cells, each rotated by a multiple of $90^\circ$, so that every internal edge joins a tab and a blank of the same type and all flat edges lie on the border. Let $k(n)$ be the least $k$ for which some $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types has exactly one assembly up to the four rotations of the whole square. Determine the order of $k(n)$; in particular, is $k(n)=\Theta(\sqrt n)$?
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M017: Blank jigsaw with few edge shapes
A blank n×n jigsaw has each internal edge cut in one of k shapes (a tab fitting only its own blank);
pieces may be rotated. How small can k be if some n×n blank jigsaw still assembles in exactly one way
(up to rotating the whole square)? Counting gives k ≥ c√n; random puzzles need about n.
Informal statement: An n×n jigsaw with k edge types assigns to each internal edge of the n×n grid a type
in [k] and an orientation (which side carries the tab); border edges are flat. Pieces are the n² unit
squares, each a distinct physical object carrying its four (type, tab/blank) labels up to rotation. An
assembly places all pieces bijectively on the cells, each rotated by a multiple of 90°, so that every
internal edge joins a tab and a blank of the same type and all flat edges lie on the border. Let k(n)
be the least k for which some n×n jigsaw with k edge types has exactly one assembly up to the four
rotations of the whole square. Is k(n) = Θ(√n)? Since k(n) ≥ c√n is known (unique assembly forces
all n² pieces to be distinct), Claim is the upper bound k(n) = O(√n).
Formalization notes: Cells are `Fin n × Fin n` (row, column; row 0 on top). Sides are `Fin 4` in
clockwise order 0 = N, 1 = E, 2 = S, 3 = W. A side label is `none` (flat) or `some (t, b)` with type
`t : Fin k` and `b = true` for a tab. `Valid L`: flat exactly on the border, and horizontally /
vertically adjacent cells show the same type with opposite tab/blank. A jigsaw is a valid labelling
`side` of the solved grid; piece p is cell p of the solved grid. An assembly is `(σ, r)`: piece p goes
to cell σ p rotated clockwise r p quarter-turns, so cell c shows on side d the label
`side (σ⁻¹ c) (d − r (σ⁻¹ c))`. Rotating a valid assembly as a whole gives a valid assembly with every
r increased by 1, so the four global rotations of the solved assembly are always 4 distinct
assemblies; "exactly one assembly up to rotation" ⇔ the number of valid assemblies is exactly 4.
Proving `Claim` = ∃ C, ∀ n ≥ 1, a uniquely assembling n×n jigsaw with ≤ C√n edge types.
Proving `¬Claim` = k(n)/√n is unbounded.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM017

/-- Cells of the n×n grid. -/
abbrev Cell (n : ℕ) : Type := Fin n × Fin n

/-- Side label: flat (`none`) or (type, is-tab). -/
abbrev Label (k : ℕ) : Type := Option (Fin k × Bool)

/-- Two sides fit: same type, one tab and one blank. -/
def Fits {k : ℕ} (x y : Label k) : Prop :=
  ∃ t : Fin k, ∃ b : Bool, x = some (t, b) ∧ y = some (t, !b)

/-- Side `d` of cell `c` is on the outer border. -/
def OnBorder {n : ℕ} (c : Cell n) (d : Fin 4) : Prop :=
  (d = 0 ∧ (c.1 : ℕ) = 0) ∨ (d = 1 ∧ (c.2 : ℕ) + 1 = n) ∨
  (d = 2 ∧ (c.1 : ℕ) + 1 = n) ∨ (d = 3 ∧ (c.2 : ℕ) = 0)

/-- A labelling of the sides of all cells is a correctly fitted puzzle. -/
def Valid {n k : ℕ} (L : Cell n → Fin 4 → Label k) : Prop :=
  (∀ (c : Cell n) (d : Fin 4), L c d = none ↔ OnBorder c d) ∧
  (∀ c c' : Cell n, c.1 = c'.1 → (c.2 : ℕ) + 1 = (c'.2 : ℕ) → Fits (L c 1) (L c' 3)) ∧
  (∀ c c' : Cell n, c.2 = c'.2 → (c.1 : ℕ) + 1 = (c'.1 : ℕ) → Fits (L c 2) (L c' 0))

/-- Labels shown on the grid when piece `p` is put at cell `σ p`, rotated by `r p` quarter-turns. -/
def placed {n k : ℕ} (side : Cell n → Fin 4 → Label k)
    (a : Equiv.Perm (Cell n) × (Cell n → Fin 4)) : Cell n → Fin 4 → Label k :=
  fun c d => side (a.1.symm c) (d - a.2 (a.1.symm c))

/-- Number of valid assemblies of the jigsaw `side`. -/
noncomputable def numAssemblies {n k : ℕ} (side : Cell n → Fin 4 → Label k) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card {a : Equiv.Perm (Cell n) × (Cell n → Fin 4) // Valid (placed side a)}

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → ∃ k : ℕ, (k : ℝ) ≤ C * Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) ∧
    ∃ side : Cell n → Fin 4 → Label k, Valid side ∧ numAssemblies side = 4

end OpenProblems.QEDM017
prov_reason: This is a deterministic-design version of the random jigsaw unique-reconstruction thresholds; the searches found no source posing the designed minimum k(n).

title: Breaking the log k barrier for 3-petal sunflowers
credit: Erdős-Rado 1960 (sunflower conjecture); log k barrier discussed in Alweiss-Lovett-Wu-Zhang, Annals 2021, and Rao, The story of sunflowers, JLMS 2026 (arXiv:2509.14790)
plain: Show every family of more than (o(log k))^k sets of size k (e.g. (log k)^{(1-c)k} or (log log k)^{O(k)}) contains a sunflower with 3 petals.
math: Let f(k,3) be the least m such that every family of m distinct k-element sets contains a 3-petal sunflower. Known: f(k,3) <= (C log k)^k (ALWZ, Rao, Bell-Chueluecha-Warnke). Prove f(k,3) <= (eps(k) log k)^k for some eps(k)->0, e.g. f(k,3) <= (log k)^{(1-c)k} for a constant c>0.
refs: Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, Zhang, Improved bounds for the sunflower lemma, Annals of Math 2021
Bell, Chueluecha, Warnke, Note on sunflowers, Discrete Math 2021
Rao, The story of sunflowers, JLMS 2026 / arXiv:2509.14790
Lovett, PCMI lecture notes: from sunflowers to thresholds

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M018: Breaking the log k barrier for 3-petal sunflowers
Let f(k,3) be the least m such that every family of m distinct k-element sets contains three
sets whose pairwise intersections all coincide (a 3-petal sunflower). The best known bound is
f(k,3) <= (C log k)^k (Alweiss-Lovett-Wu-Zhang, Rao, Bell-Chueluecha-Warnke). The problem asks
to beat the log k barrier: f(k,3) <= (eps(k) log k)^k with eps(k) -> 0.
Informal statement: Let f(k,3) be the least m such that every family of m distinct k-element
sets contains a 3-petal sunflower. Prove f(k,3) <= (eps(k) log k)^k for some eps(k) -> 0
(e.g. f(k,3) <= (log k)^{(1-c)k}).
Formalization notes: Sets are finite subsets of ℕ (the ground set is irrelevant, since any
finite family lives on a finite ground set). A 3-petal sunflower is three pairwise distinct
members A, B, C with A ∩ B = A ∩ C = B ∩ C. "f(k,3) <= (eps(k) log k)^k for some eps(k) -> 0"
is encoded in the equivalent form: for every ε > 0 there is K such that for all k >= K every
family of k-sets of size strictly greater than (ε log k)^k contains a 3-petal sunflower.
Proving Claim breaks the log k barrier; proving ¬Claim shows there is ε > 0 and infinitely many
k with sunflower-free families of more than (ε log k)^k k-sets, i.e. that
f(k,3) >= (ε log k)^k infinitely often (this would refute the Erdős-Rado sunflower conjecture
for 3 petals). Known: f(k,3) <= (C log k)^k.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM018

/-- Three sets form a sunflower with 3 petals: they are pairwise distinct and all pairwise
intersections coincide. -/
def IsSunflower3 (A B C : Finset ℕ) : Prop :=
  A ≠ B ∧ A ≠ C ∧ B ≠ C ∧ A ∩ B = A ∩ C ∧ A ∩ B = B ∩ C

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ K : ℕ, ∀ k : ℕ, K ≤ k →
    ∀ F : Finset (Finset ℕ), (∀ A ∈ F, A.card = k) →
      (ε * Real.log (k : ℝ)) ^ k < (F.card : ℝ) →
        ∃ A ∈ F, ∃ B ∈ F, ∃ C ∈ F, IsSunflower3 A B C

end OpenProblems.QEDM018
prov_reason: Beating the (log k)^k barrier for 3-petal sunflowers is an explicitly discussed open step toward the Erdős-Rado conjecture in the sunflower literature (ALWZ, Lovett notes, Rao survey); QED did not originate it.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M019: Codes avoiding square distances
Let A(n) be the largest size of a set of binary strings of length n in which no two distinct
strings differ in a perfect-square number of positions (1, 4, 9, 16, ...). This is a
Hamming-cube analogue of the Sarkozy-Furstenberg theorem on sets without square differences.
Known: exp(c n^{1/3}) <= A(n) <= (2 - delta)^n. The core open question is whether A(n) grows
exponentially or is 2^{o(n)}.
Informal statement: Let A(n) = max{|C| : C ⊆ {0,1}^n, d_H(x,y) ∉ {1,4,9,16,...} for all x ≠ y in C}.
Decide whether A(n) = 2^{o(n)}, i.e. whether limsup (1/n) log_2 A(n) = 0.
Formalization notes: Binary strings are `Fin n → Bool`; `hamming x y` counts coordinates where
they differ. `SquareAvoiding C` says every pair of distinct elements of the finite set `C` has a
Hamming distance that is not a perfect square (`IsSquare` on ℕ; distance 0 never occurs for
distinct strings). To avoid junk values of `sSup`, the claim quantifies over all square-avoiding
codes directly: `Claim` says that for every ε > 0, for all sufficiently large n, every
square-avoiding code in {0,1}^n has at most 2^{εn} elements, i.e. A(n) = 2^{o(n)}
(subexponential). Proving `Claim` shows subexponential growth; proving `¬Claim` shows there are
ε > 0 and infinitely many n with a square-avoiding code of size > 2^{εn}, i.e.
limsup (1/n) log_2 A(n) > 0. The finer question of whether liminf = limsup is not formalized here.
Known bounds (not part of the claim): A(n) ≥ exp(c n^{1/3}) via constant-weight codes with all
distances strictly between consecutive squares; A(n) ≤ (2 - δ)^n via Frankl-Rödl.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM019

/-- Hamming distance between two binary strings of length `n`. -/
def hamming {n : ℕ} (x y : Fin n → Bool) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter (fun i : Fin n => x i ≠ y i)).card

/-- A code is square-avoiding if no two distinct codewords are at perfect-square Hamming distance. -/
def SquareAvoiding {n : ℕ} (C : Finset (Fin n → Bool)) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ C, ∀ y ∈ C, x ≠ y → ¬ IsSquare (hamming x y)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n →
    ∀ C : Finset (Fin n → Bool), SquareAvoiding C →
      (C.card : ℝ) ≤ (2 : ℝ) ^ (ε * (n : ℝ))

end OpenProblems.QEDM019
prov_reason: Reviewer notes found no literature forbidding square (or any infinite sparse) set of distances in the Hamming cube; the question is QED's transfer of Sarkozy's theorem to {0,1}^n.

title: Critical linear firefighter rate on Z^3
credit: Extension of Develin-Hartke (arXiv:math/0409195) and Dyer-Martinez-Pedroza-Thorne (arXiv:1507.03050, Cor. 4); o(t) failure from arXiv:2002.11205.
results: c* >= 8/243 (~0.033), elementary: Loomis-Whitney gives |vertex boundary of B| >= |B|^{2/3}; for c<2a^2-6a^3 with a=2/9, a large initial cube burns forever by induction b_t >= (a(t+T0))^3. Using the asymptotically sharp Wang-Wang vertex isoperimetry (l1-balls, constant 4(3/4)^{2/3}) the same argument heuristically gives ~32/27, not checked rigorously c* <= 8, elementary: protect the l1-sphere |x|_1=D (4D^2+2 vertices) before step D-R; c>8 suffices for large D.
plain: On the 3D grid, a finite fire spreads to all unprotected neighbours each step, and at step t you may protect about ct new vertices. It is known that linear growth is the right order. Elementary arguments show that rate c>8 always contains the fire and that c<32/27 does not. Narrow this gap, or find the exact critical rate.
math: Let c* = inf{c : for every finite initial fire B_0 ⊂ Z^3 there is a protection schedule with at most ⌊ct⌋ newly protected vertices at step t that keeps the total burnt set finite}. Elementary: the growth recursion |B_{t+1}| ≥ |B_t| + |∂B_t| − c(t+1)(t+2)/2 with the Wang–Wang vertex-isoperimetric inequality in Z^3 gives c* ≥ 32/27; numerics suggest a static wall gives c* ≲ 6.4. Target: prove c* > 32/27, i.e. some rate c > 32/27 fails to contain some finite outbreak.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M020: Critical linear firefighter rate on Z^3
On Z^3 a finite fire spreads each step to all unprotected neighbours, and at step t one may protect about ct new vertices. Linear rate is the right order; the question is the critical constant c*. This file asks to improve the stated lower bound.
Informal statement: Let c* = inf{c : for every finite initial fire B_0 ⊂ Z^3 there is a protection schedule with at most ⌊c t⌋ newly protected vertices at step t that keeps the total burnt set finite}. Known (QED-derived, elementary): 8/243 ≤ c* ≤ 8 (bound field and W); M additionally records 64/243 ≤ c* ≤ 48/7 (not independently checked here; numerics suggest a static ℓ^4-ball wall gives ≈ 6.4). Target: prove c* > 32/27, i.e. some rate c > 32/27 fails to contain some finite outbreak.
Note: c* ≥ 32/27 already follows from the growth recursion |B_{t+1}| ≥ |B_t| + |∂B_t| − c(t+1)(t+2)/2 together with the
Wang–Wang vertex-isoperimetric inequality in Z^3 (|∂A| ≳ 4(3|A|/4)^{2/3}); the 64/243 bound is the same argument with the
Loomis–Whitney constant |∂A| ≥ 2|A|^{2/3}. So 64/243 is not a meaningful target.
Formalization notes: Fire dynamics: step t+1 = protect P(t+1), then spread to unprotected neighbours; protected vertices stay protected forever; protecting an already burnt vertex is allowed but useless, and re-protecting wastes budget, so allowing arbitrary sets of size ≤ c·s is equivalent to the usual rules. The fire is deterministic, so adaptive strategies are the same as fixed schedules P : ℕ → Finset V3. Budget at step 0 is 0. Containment = the union of all burnt sets is finite (equivalently, the fire stops). Contains is monotone in c, so c* > 32/27 ⇔ ∃ c > 32/27, ¬Contains c. The lower bound is the formalized side because the upper side is essentially settled numerically (≈6.4 wall). Proving ¬Claim means every rate c > 32/27 contains all finite outbreaks, i.e. c* ≤ 32/27 (hence = 32/27).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM020

/-- The vertices of the grid `Z^3`. -/
abbrev V3 : Type := ℤ × ℤ × ℤ

/-- Grid adjacency: `ℓ¹` distance exactly `1`. -/
def Adj3 (u v : V3) : Prop :=
  |u.1 - v.1| + |u.2.1 - v.2.1| + |u.2.2 - v.2.2| = 1

/-- The burnt set after `t` steps, starting from the fire `B0`, when the set `P s` is protected at step
`s ≥ 1`. At step `t + 1` the firefighters first protect `P (t + 1)`; then the fire spreads to every
neighbour of a burnt vertex that has not been protected at any step `≤ t + 1`. -/
def burnt (B0 : Set V3) (P : ℕ → Finset V3) : ℕ → Set V3
  | 0 => B0
  | t + 1 => burnt B0 P t ∪
      {v : V3 | (∀ s : ℕ, s ≤ t + 1 → v ∉ P s) ∧ ∃ u ∈ burnt B0 P t, Adj3 u v}

/-- Rate `c` contains every finite outbreak: for every finite initial fire there is a schedule with
at most `c * s` (equivalently `⌊c s⌋`) vertices protected at step `s` such that only finitely many
vertices ever burn. -/
def Contains (c : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ B0 : Finset V3, ∃ P : ℕ → Finset V3,
    (∀ s : ℕ, ((P s).card : ℝ) ≤ c * (s : ℝ)) ∧
    (⋃ t : ℕ, burnt (↑B0 : Set V3) P t).Finite

/-- `c* > 32/27`: some rate above `32/27` does not contain every finite outbreak. -/
def Claim : Prop := ∃ c : ℝ, 32 / 27 < c ∧ ¬ Contains c

end OpenProblems.QEDM020
M_fix_reason: M (64/243 ≤ c* ≤ 48/7) contradicts W and the bound field (8/243 ≤ c* ≤ 8, with 8/243 = 2a^2-6a^3 at a=2/9 checked), and M never defines c* or the target; the fix states c*, both versions of the known bounds, and a single open target that improves on either.
prov_reason: Linear order t^{d-2} of firefighters on Z^3 is known; asking for the sharp constant is a new parameter question formulated by QED.

title: Distinct character degrees of the symmetric group
credit: On the irreducible character degrees of symmetric groups and their multiplicities, arXiv:2410.01726 (2024)
premise_risks: arXiv:2410.01726 (preprint, refereeing status unclear): the numerical data for n <= 129 and the suggested limit near 2.5 are context only; Claim does not depend on them.
plain: Conjugate partitions always give representations of S_n of the same dimension, so at most about half of the p(n) irreducible representations can have distinct dimensions. Decide whether the fraction of distinct dimensions tends to a limit, and whether that limit is positive.
math: Let d(n) = #{f^λ : λ ⊢ n} be the number of distinct irreducible character degrees of S_n and p(n) the number of partitions of n. Prove or disprove: d(n)/p(n) converges to a positive limit L as n → ∞.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M021: Distinct character degrees of the symmetric group
Conjugate partitions give irreducible representations of S_n of the same dimension, so at most
about half of the p(n) irreducible representations have distinct dimensions. Does the fraction
d(n)/p(n) of distinct dimensions tend to a positive limit?
Informal statement: Let d(n) = #{f^λ : λ ⊢ n} be the number of distinct irreducible character degrees of S_n and p(n) the number of partitions of n. Prove or disprove: d(n)/p(n) converges to a positive limit L as n → ∞.
Formalization notes: The original asks to determine whether lim d(n)/p(n) exists, find it, and
in particular decide whether liminf d(n)/p(n) > 0. Claim is the natural conjecture "the limit
exists and is positive". Proving ¬Claim means: either d(n)/p(n) does not converge, or it
converges to 0. Partitions of n are generated explicitly as weakly decreasing lists of positive
integers summing to n (`partitionsList n`; first part k+1 <= m, remaining parts <= k+1). The
degree f^λ is defined by the hook length formula f^λ = n! / Π_{cells} hook(cell), where the hook
of cell (i,j) is (λ_i - j - 1) + #{k > i : λ_k > j} + 1; the division is exact by the hook length
theorem, so this is the number of standard Young tableaux, i.e. the dimension of the Specht
module. d(n) counts distinct values of this list, p(n) its length (p(n) >= 1). Data: p(40) =
37338, d(40) = 16216 (checked with an independent script implementing these exact definitions);
d(n)/p(n) ∈ [0.40, 0.47] for 20 <= n <= 45; arXiv:2410.01726 suggests p(n)/d(n) may tend to
about 2.5 (a referee suggested π√(2/3)), but this is not part of Claim.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM021

/-- `partitionsAux fuel n m`: all partitions of `n` into parts `<= m`, as weakly decreasing lists.
`fuel` only guarantees termination; `fuel >= n` suffices. -/
def partitionsAux : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → List (List ℕ)
  | 0, n, _ => if n = 0 then [[]] else []
  | fuel + 1, n, m =>
    if n = 0 then [[]] else
      (List.range (min m n)).flatMap (fun k =>
        (partitionsAux fuel (n - (k + 1)) (k + 1)).map (fun l => (k + 1) :: l))

/-- All partitions of `n`, each listed once as a weakly decreasing list of positive parts. -/
def partitionsList (n : ℕ) : List (List ℕ) := partitionsAux n n n

/-- Product of all hook lengths of the Young diagram with row lengths `l`. -/
def hookProduct (l : List ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ∏ i ∈ Finset.range l.length, ∏ j ∈ Finset.range (l.getD i 0),
    ((l.getD i 0 - j - 1) + ((l.drop (i + 1)).filter (fun r => decide (j < r))).length + 1)

/-- Degree of the irreducible character of S_n indexed by `l`, via the hook length formula. -/
def charDegree (n : ℕ) (l : List ℕ) : ℕ := n.factorial / hookProduct l

/-- p(n), the number of partitions of n. -/
def numPartitions (n : ℕ) : ℕ := (partitionsList n).length

/-- d(n), the number of distinct irreducible character degrees of S_n. -/
def numDistinctDegrees (n : ℕ) : ℕ := ((partitionsList n).map (charDegree n)).dedup.length

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ L : ℝ, 0 < L ∧
    Filter.Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (numDistinctDegrees n : ℝ) / (numPartitions n : ℝ))
      Filter.atTop (nhds L)

end OpenProblems.QEDM021
M_fix_reason: M is a 'determine whether / find' question. Turned into the single conjecture 'the limit exists and is positive'. The intermediate question liminf > 0 is not separately encoded.
prov_reason: Reviewer notes: already posed in essence in arXiv:2410.01726, which plots p(n)/|cd(S_n)| to n=129, says it is unclear whether a limit exists, and records a referee's guess π√(2/3).

title: Is the Petersen graph common?
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.20149 (2026 preprint): cited background on common graphs; M does not depend on it.
plain: Color the edges of a huge complete graph red and blue. Does a random coloring minimize the number of single-color copies of the Petersen graph?
math: Let $P$ be the Petersen graph ($10$ vertices, $15$ edges) and $m(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{\chi}\frac{\#\{\text{monochromatic copies of }P\text{ in }(K_n,\chi)\}}{\#\{\text{copies of }P\text{ in }K_n\}}$, minimum over red/blue colorings $\chi$ of $E(K_n)$. Is $m(P)=2^{-14}$, i.e. is $P$ common? Equivalently, is $t(P,W)+t(P,1-W)\ge 2^{-14}$ for every graphon $W$? If not, determine $m(P)$.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M022: Is the Petersen graph common?
Colour the edges of a huge complete graph red and blue. Does a uniformly random colouring
asymptotically minimise the number of monochromatic copies of the Petersen graph?
Informal statement: Let P be the Petersen graph (10 vertices, 15 edges). Is P common, i.e. is
t(P,W) + t(P,1−W) ≥ 2^{−14} for every graphon W? (Equivalently m(P) = 2^{−14}, where m(P) is
the limiting minimum fraction of monochromatic copies of P over red/blue colourings of K_n.)
Formalization notes: Petersen graph on `Fin 10`: outer cycle 0-1-2-3-4-0, spokes i–(i+5),
inner pentagram 5-7-9-6-8-5, given as a list of 15 edges. For a symmetric n × n array A with
entries in [0,1] (a step graphon with n equal parts, diagonal allowed), the homomorphism count
hom(P,A) = ∑_{φ : Fin 10 → Fin n} ∏_{ij ∈ E(P)} A(φ i, φ j) equals n^{10} · t(P, W_A). Since
step graphons are dense in the cut metric and t(P,·) is cut-continuous, "∀ graphons W" is
equivalent to "∀ n, ∀ such A". The complement is the entrywise array 1 − A(i,j) (written as a
function, not Matrix subtraction, to avoid the identity matrix). Proving `Claim` = P is common;
`¬Claim` = an explicit (step) graphon beating the random colouring, i.e. P is uncommon.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM022

/-- The 15 edges of the Petersen graph on `Fin 10`. -/
def petersenEdges : List (Fin 10 × Fin 10) :=
  [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 0),
   (0, 5), (1, 6), (2, 7), (3, 8), (4, 9),
   (5, 7), (7, 9), (9, 6), (6, 8), (8, 5)]

/-- Homomorphism count of the Petersen graph into the weighted graph `A`. -/
def homP {n : ℕ} (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ φ : Fin 10 → Fin n, (petersenEdges.map (fun e => A (φ e.1) (φ e.2))).prod

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ (n : ℕ) (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℝ),
    (∀ i j, A i j = A j i) → (∀ i j, 0 ≤ A i j ∧ A i j ≤ 1) →
    (1 / 2 : ℝ) ^ 14 * (n : ℝ) ^ 10 ≤ homP A + homP (fun i j => 1 - A i j)

end OpenProblems.QEDM022
M_fix_reason: M (already rewritten as the commonness question) is correct; 'if not, determine m(P)' is a fallback and not formalized.
prov_reason: Commonness of specific graphs is a classical programme, but no source found posing or settling the Petersen graph specifically (one search, plus refs).

title: Monochromatic square-sum triangles, many colours
credit: Khalfalah–Szemerédi (2006), monochromatic x+y = z² for finite colourings.
plain: Colour the positive integers with finitely many colours. Show there are always three different numbers of the same colour whose three pairwise sums are all perfect squares.
math: Prove that for every $r\ge1$ and every colouring $\chi:\mathbb N\to\{1,\dots,r\}$ there exist distinct $a,b,c\in\mathbb N$ with $\chi(a)=\chi(b)=\chi(c)$ and $a+b,\ a+c,\ b+c$ all perfect squares. (Equivalently: the triangle hypergraph of the graph on $\mathbb N$ with $a\sim b\iff a+b=\square$ has infinite chromatic number.)

/-! QED-M023: Monochromatic square-sum triangles, many colours
Colour the positive integers with finitely many colours. Show there are always three distinct
numbers of the same colour whose three pairwise sums are all perfect squares.
Informal statement: For every r ≥ 1 and every colouring χ : ℕ → {1,…,r} there exist distinct
positive integers a, b, c with χ(a) = χ(b) = χ(c) and a+b, a+c, b+c all perfect squares.
Formalization notes:
* Colours are `Fin r`; the integers are naturals required to be positive (0 is excluded, as

title: Paley spin glass
results: Correct. Q is circulant with eigenvalues chi(a)sqrt p (Gauss sums), so E_p<=p^{3/2}/2. Square-wave ratio is (4/pi^2)sum_{m odd}chi(m)/m^2 + o(1); taking p=1 mod 8 and p=1 mod q for odd q<=y (reciprocity + Dirichlet) gives limsup=1/2. Recomputed p=53881: 0.4925. Bonus: the sum is >=2-pi^2/8 so liminf>=0.31.
plain: Place a ±1 spin at each element of F_p, and let each pair interact through the Legendre symbol of their difference. Equivalently, this is the max-cut problem for the Paley graph. The eigenvalue bound caps the ground-state energy at p^{3/2}/2. Simple square-wave configurations reach this bound along special primes, but heuristic search for typical primes stalls around 0.46. Is the eigenvalue bound asymptotically sharp for all primes?
math: For primes $p\equiv1\pmod4$ let $E_p=\max_{\sigma\in\{\pm1\}^{\mathbb F_p}}\sum_{i<j}\left(\frac{j-i}{p}\right)\sigma_i\sigma_j$. The circulant matrix $Q=\big(\big(\frac{j-i}p\big)\big)_{i,j\in\mathbb F_p}$ is symmetric with eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt p$ (each with multiplicity $\frac{p-1}2$) and $0$, so $E_p\le\frac12p^{3/2}$. (For the Paley graph $P_p$, $\mathrm{surp}(P_p)=\mathrm{maxcut}(P_p)-\frac12|E(P_p)|\le \frac14E_p+\frac p8$.) It is known that $\limsup_p E_p/p^{3/2}=\frac12$: if $(\frac qp)=1$ for all primes $q\le y$, then $\sigma_x=\operatorname{sgn}\cos(2\pi x/p)$ has ratio $\frac12-o_y(1)$; and the same $\sigma$ gives $E_p/p^{3/2}\ge\frac4{\pi^2}\big(2-\frac{\pi^2}8\big)-o(1)\approx0.31$ for every $p$. Determine $\liminf_{p}E_p/p^{3/2}$; in particular, is it $\frac12$?

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M024: Paley spin glass
Put a ±1 spin on each element of F_p (p ≡ 1 mod 4) and let each pair interact via the Legendre symbol of their difference. The spectral bound gives ground-state energy E_p ≤ p^{3/2}/2, attained asymptotically along special primes. Is it asymptotically attained for all primes?
Informal statement: For primes $p\equiv1\pmod4$ let $E_p=\max_{\sigma\in\{\pm1\}^{\mathbb F_p}}\sum_{i<j}\left(\frac{j-i}{p}\right)\sigma_i\sigma_j$. The circulant matrix $Q=\big(\big(\frac{j-i}p\big)\big)_{i,j\in\mathbb F_p}$ is symmetric with eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt p$ (each with multiplicity $\frac{p-1}2$) and $0$, so $E_p\le\frac12p^{3/2}$. (For the Paley graph $P_p$, $\mathrm{surp}(P_p)=\mathrm{maxcut}(P_p)-\frac12|E(P_p)|\le \frac14E_p+\frac p8$.) It is known that $\limsup_p E_p/p^{3/2}=\frac12$: if $(\frac qp)=1$ for all primes $q\le y$, then $\sigma_x=\operatorname{sgn}\cos(2\pi x/p)$ has ratio $\frac12-o_y(1)$; and the same $\sigma$ gives $E_p/p^{3/2}\ge\frac4{\pi^2}\big(2-\frac{\pi^2}8\big)-o(1)\approx0.31$ for every $p$. Determine $\liminf_{p}E_p/p^{3/2}$; in particular, is it $\frac12$?
Formalization notes: Elements of F_p are represented by Fin p; for i<j the difference j-i is a natural in [1,p-1], so no ℕ-subtraction junk occurs. The Legendre symbol is defined from scratch (chi) to avoid needing a Fact p.Prime instance. E_p is the max of energy over s : Fin p → Bool; instead of the max, Claim asserts existence of a good configuration, which is equivalent. Known: E_p ≤ p^{3/2}/2 for all such p, limsup E_p/p^{3/2} = 1/2, and liminf ≥ 0.31 (square-wave configuration). Claim is 'liminf = 1/2'. Proving ¬Claim means exhibiting ε>0 and infinitely many primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 with E_p < (1/2-ε)p^{3/2}.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM024

/-- `d` is a square modulo `p` (for `p ∤ d` this means `d` is a quadratic residue). -/
def IsSqMod (p d : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ x : ℕ, x ^ 2 % p = d % p

open Classical in
/-- The Legendre symbol `(d / p)`, defined from scratch: `0` if `p ∣ d`, `1` if `d` is a nonzero
square mod `p`, and `-1` otherwise. -/
noncomputable def chi (p d : ℕ) : ℤ :=
  if d % p = 0 then 0 else if IsSqMod p d then 1 else -1

/-- The spin `±1` attached to a Boolean. -/
def spin (b : Bool) : ℤ := if b then 1 else -1

/-- The energy `∑_{i<j} ((j-i)/p) σ_i σ_j` of a spin configuration on `{0, …, p-1} ≅ F_p`. -/
noncomputable def energy (p : ℕ) (s : Fin p → Bool) : ℤ :=
  ∑ i : Fin p, ∑ j : Fin p,
    if i.val < j.val then chi p (j.val - i.val) * spin (s i) * spin (s j) else 0

/-- `liminf_{p ≡ 1 (mod 4)} E_p / p^{3/2} = 1/2`. Since `E_p ≤ p^{3/2}/2` always, this says: for every
`ε > 0`, all sufficiently large primes `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)` admit a configuration with energy at least
`(1/2 - ε) p^{3/2}`. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ P₀ : ℕ, ∀ p : ℕ, Nat.Prime p → p % 4 = 1 → P₀ ≤ p →
    ∃ s : Fin p → Bool, ((1 : ℝ) / 2 - ε) * ((p : ℝ) * Real.sqrt (p : ℝ)) ≤ (energy p s : ℝ)

end OpenProblems.QEDM024
prov_reason: No literature on max-cut / ground states of the Paley graph Legendre-symbol spin glass was found; the question is QED's.

title: Periodic optimal colourings of Cayley graphs of Z^2
credit: Posed for lattice Cayley graphs in 'The chromatic number of 4-dimensional lattices', arXiv:2407.03513 (2024); related: periodic colourings of quasi-transitive graphs, arXiv:2411.01951 (2024).
results: No proof is claimed. The decidability corollary is correct: compactness (de Bruijn-Erdos) semi-decides chi>k, and enumerating periodic colourings (torus quotients) semi-decides chi<=k if the answer is yes. A Z^2 SFT with one period also has a fully periodic point, so 'periodic point' is unambiguous here.
premise_risks: arXiv:2607.26942 (2026 preprint) is in refs; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Join two points of the integer grid when their difference lies in a fixed finite set D. If this graph can be properly coloured with k colours, can it always be coloured with k colours in a repeating, wallpaper-like pattern? On a line the answer is yes. For some infinite graphs built from trees it is no. The plane is the first open case, and a yes would also give an algorithm for the chromatic number.
math: For finite symmetric $D\subset\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}$ let $G_D=\mathrm{Cay}(\mathbb Z^2,D)$ with $\chi(G_D)=k<\infty$. Must $G_D$ have a proper $k$-colouring invariant under a finite-index subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$? Equivalently, does the $k$-colouring subshift $X_{D,k}\subset\{1..k\}^{\mathbb Z^2}$ always contain a periodic point? (A yes makes $\{(D,k):\chi(G_D)\le k\}$ decidable via compactness plus enumeration of periodic colourings. A no gives the first weakly aperiodic colouring subshift on $\mathbb Z^2$.) Same question for $\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge3$.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M025: Periodic optimal colourings of Cayley graphs of Z^2
Join two points of ℤ² when their difference lies in a fixed finite set D. If this graph can be
properly coloured with k colours, can it always be properly coloured with k colours in a doubly
periodic pattern?
Informal statement: For finite symmetric D ⊂ ℤ² \ {0} let G_D = Cay(ℤ², D) with χ(G_D) = k.
Must G_D have a proper k-colouring invariant under a finite-index subgroup of ℤ²?
(Equivalently, does the k-colouring subshift X_{D,k} always contain a periodic point?)
Formalization notes:
* A proper k-colouring is `c : ℤ × ℤ → Fin k` with `c (v + d) ≠ c v` for all v and d ∈ D.
* Invariance under a finite-index subgroup Λ ≤ ℤ² is equivalent to invariance under N·ℤ² for
  some N ≥ 1 (every finite-index subgroup contains N·ℤ², N = index), which is what
  `IsPeriodicColouring` states.
* The claim is stated for every k admitting a proper k-colouring rather than only k = χ(G_D);
  this is equivalent: k = χ is a special case, and a periodic χ-colouring is a periodic
  k-colouring for every k ≥ χ. (χ(G_D) is always finite for finite D.)
* Proving `Claim`: every such colouring problem on ℤ² that is solvable has a periodic solution.
  Proving `¬Claim`: some D, k admit proper k-colourings but no periodic one.
* Only the ℤ² question is formalized (the ℤ^d, d ≥ 3, version is a follow-up).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM025

/-- `c` is a proper colouring of `Cay(ℤ², D)` with `k` colours. -/
def IsProperColouring (D : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) (k : ℕ) (c : ℤ × ℤ → Fin k) : Prop :=
  ∀ v : ℤ × ℤ, ∀ d : ℤ × ℤ, d ∈ D → c (v + d) ≠ c v

/-- `c` is invariant under translation by `N·ℤ²` for some `N ≥ 1`. -/
def IsPeriodicColouring {k : ℕ} (c : ℤ × ℤ → Fin k) : Prop :=
  ∃ N : ℕ, 0 < N ∧ ∀ v : ℤ × ℤ,
    c (v + ((N : ℤ), (0 : ℤ))) = c v ∧ c (v + ((0 : ℤ), (N : ℤ))) = c v

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ D : Finset (ℤ × ℤ), (0 : ℤ × ℤ) ∉ D → (∀ d : ℤ × ℤ, d ∈ D → -d ∈ D) →
    ∀ k : ℕ, (∃ c : ℤ × ℤ → Fin k, IsProperColouring D k c) →
      ∃ c : ℤ × ℤ → Fin k, IsProperColouring D k c ∧ IsPeriodicColouring c

end OpenProblems.QEDM025
M_fix_reason: M is precise. The 'why' wrongly says 2411.01951 leaves 1-ended graphs open; it gives 1-ended counterexamples (Thompson V GRRs) and leaves only 1-ended planar graphs open. Fix the 'why'.
prov_reason: Reviewer notes that arXiv:2407.03513 (The chromatic number of 4-dimensional lattices) already poses the existence of periodic optimal colourings / computability of χ for lattice Cayley graphs as open; the ℤ² case is the base instance.

title: The complex of planar graphs
plain: Planar graphs on n labelled vertices form a simplicial complex, because deleting an edge keeps a graph planar. It is pure, since every maximal planar graph has 3n-6 edges. Its homology turns out not to be that of a wedge of top-dimensional spheres: already for n=6 it is concentrated two degrees lower and has 2-torsion. Determine its homology.
math: Let $\Pi_n$ be the simplicial complex on vertex set $E(K_n)$ whose faces are edge sets of planar graphs; it is pure of dimension $3n-7$. Determine $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Z)$, or at least $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Q)$, for all $n$. Known: $\Pi_4$ is a simplex, $\Pi_5=\partial\Delta^9\cong S^8$. For $n=6$ (computed exactly): $\tilde H_*(\Pi_6;\mathbb Q)$ is $\mathbb Q^{15}$ in degree $9=3n-9$ and $0$ elsewhere; $\tilde H_*(\Pi_6;\mathbb F_2)$ is $\mathbb F_2^{15},\mathbb F_2,\mathbb F_2$ in degrees $9,10,11$, so $\tilde H_{10}(\Pi_6;\mathbb Z)$ has $2$-torsion and $\Pi_6$ is not a wedge of spheres. The mod-2 top class is the sum of all triangulations: every face of dimension $3n-8$ of $\Pi_6$ lies in an even number (2 or 4) of facets. Questions: (a) is $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Q)$ concentrated in degree $3n-9$ for all $n\ge6$, and what is its rank and $S_n$-module structure? (b) Is $\tilde H_{3n-7}(\Pi_n;\mathbb F_2)\ne0$ for all $n\ge5$? Is all torsion 2-torsion?

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M026: The complex of planar graphs
Planar graphs on n labelled vertices form a simplicial complex Πₙ on the vertex set E(Kₙ) (deleting an edge keeps a graph
planar); it is pure of dimension 3n − 7. For n = 6 its rational reduced homology is ℚ^15 in degree 9 = 3n − 9 and zero
elsewhere, while its mod-2 homology also has classes in degrees 10 and 11, so it is not a wedge of spheres.
Informal statement: Let Πₙ be the simplicial complex on vertex set E(Kₙ) whose faces are edge sets of planar graphs.
Determine H̃_*(Πₙ; ℤ), or at least H̃_*(Πₙ; ℚ). Main question (a): is H̃_*(Πₙ; ℚ) concentrated in degree 3n − 9 for all
n ≥ 6? (Further: its rank and Sₙ-module structure; whether H̃_{3n−7}(Πₙ; 𝔽₂) ≠ 0 for all n ≥ 5; whether all torsion is
2-torsion.)
Formalization notes: Claim formalizes question (a) only (the main yes/no question): for all n ≥ 6 the rational reduced
Betti numbers vanish in every degree other than 3n − 9 ("concentrated" does not assert non-vanishing there).
Edges of Kₙ are pairs (i, j) with i < j in Fin n, linearly ordered by the key i·n + j. Planarity is defined by Wagner's
theorem: no K₅ minor and no K₃,₃ minor, where a minor model is a family of pairwise disjoint vertex sets, each inducing a
connected subgraph, with an edge between the required pairs. `Face n j` = planar edge sets of size j (simplices of
dimension j − 1; the empty face gives the augmentation, so homology is reduced). `bd n j` is the oriented boundary
matrix from size-(j+1) faces to size-j faces, with sign (−1)^(position of the removed edge). The reduced Betti number in
degree j − 1 is `redBetti n j` = dim C_j − rank(∂ out of C_j) − rank(∂ into C_j), computed over ℚ with `Matrix.rank`.
Degree 3n − 9 corresponds to face size 3n − 8. Proving Claim = concentration for all n ≥ 6; ¬Claim = some n ≥ 6 with
nonzero rational homology in another degree.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM026

/-- Edges of `Kₙ`: ordered pairs `(i, j)` with `i < j`. -/
abbrev Edge (n : ℕ) := {p : Fin n × Fin n // p.1 < p.2}

/-- A linear-order key on edges, used for orientation signs. -/
def edgeKey {n : ℕ} (e : Edge n) : ℕ := e.1.1.val * n + e.1.2.val

/-- The simple graph on `Fin n` with edge set `s`. -/
def graphOf {n : ℕ} (s : Finset (Edge n)) : SimpleGraph (Fin n) :=
  SimpleGraph.fromRel (fun u v => ∃ e ∈ s, e.1.1 = u ∧ e.1.2 = v)

/-- `G` has a `K₅` minor. -/
def HasK5Minor {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  ∃ B : Fin 5 → Set (Fin n),
    (∀ i, (SimpleGraph.induce (B i) G).Connected) ∧
    (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (B i) (B j)) ∧
    (∀ i j, i ≠ j → ∃ u ∈ B i, ∃ v ∈ B j, G.Adj u v)

/-- `G` has a `K₃,₃` minor (branch sets `0,1,2` on one side, `3,4,5` on the other). -/
def HasK33Minor {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  ∃ B : Fin 6 → Set (Fin n),
    (∀ i, (SimpleGraph.induce (B i) G).Connected) ∧
    (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (B i) (B j)) ∧
    (∀ i j : Fin 6, i.val < 3 → 3 ≤ j.val → ∃ u ∈ B i, ∃ v ∈ B j, G.Adj u v)

/-- Planarity, via Wagner's theorem. -/
def IsPlanar {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : Prop := ¬ HasK5Minor G ∧ ¬ HasK33Minor G

/-- Faces of `Πₙ` with `j` elements (simplices of dimension `j - 1`). -/
abbrev Face (n j : ℕ) := {s : Finset (Edge n) // s.card = j ∧ IsPlanar (graphOf s)}

noncomputable instance instFintypeFace (n j : ℕ) : Fintype (Face n j) := Fintype.ofFinite _

/-- Oriented boundary matrix from faces of size `j + 1` (columns) to faces of size `j` (rows). -/
noncomputable def bd (n j : ℕ) : Matrix (Face n j) (Face n (j + 1)) ℚ :=
  fun τ σ =>
    if τ.1 ⊆ σ.1 then
      (-1 : ℚ) ^ (σ.1.filter (fun f => ∀ e ∈ σ.1 \ τ.1, edgeKey f < edgeKey e)).card
    else 0

/-- Rational reduced Betti number of `Πₙ` in degree `j - 1` (faces of size `j`). -/
noncomputable def redBetti (n : ℕ) : ℕ → ℕ
  | 0 => Fintype.card (Face n 0) - (bd n 0).rank
  | (j + 1) => Fintype.card (Face n (j + 1)) - (bd n j).rank - (bd n (j + 1)).rank

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, 6 ≤ n → ∀ j : ℕ, j ≠ 3 * n - 8 → redBetti n j = 0

end OpenProblems.QEDM026
prov_reason: No literature on the simplicial complex of planar graphs was found (planarity is absent from Jonsson's survey of monotone graph properties); the question and the n = 6 data are QED's.

title: 2^{Omega(n)} hardness of Euclidean SVP under ETH
credit: Aggarwal, Gupta, Morolia, Zhang, 'Mind the Gap? Not for SVP Hardness under ETH!', ICALP 2026 (LIPIcs 374, paper 8), arXiv:2504.02695, Open Problem 1.
plain: Show that approximate SVP in the l_2 norm (some constant gamma>1) has no 2^{o(n)}-time algorithm unless (randomized) ETH fails; or identify an obstruction (e.g. for the Z^n-based gadget) showing the l_p, p>2 technique cannot reach p=2.
math: Prove there is a constant gamma > 1 such that, if randomized ETH holds (there is delta > 0 such that no bounded-error randomized algorithm decides 3-SAT on n variables in time 2^{delta n} poly(size)), then there is delta' > 0 such that no bounded-error randomized algorithm decides gamma-GapSVP in the l_2 norm on rank-n integer lattices in time 2^{delta' n} poly(size) (2^{Omega(n)} hardness, in particular no 2^{o(n)}-time algorithm). The alternative 'technique obstruction' target is a meta-statement and is not formalized.
refs: Aggarwal, Gupta, Morolia, Zhang, Mind the Gap? Not for SVP Hardness under ETH!, ICALP 2026, arXiv:2504.02695

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M027: 2^{Omega(n)} hardness of Euclidean SVP under ETH
Show that for some constant γ > 1, γ-approximate GapSVP in the ℓ₂ norm has no 2^{o(n)}-time randomized algorithm
unless randomized ETH fails; or show the AGMZ technique (Zⁿ gadget plus Theta-function inequality, valid for p > 2)
provably cannot reach p = 2.
Informal statement: Prove there is a constant γ > 1 such that, if randomized ETH holds (there is δ > 0 such that
no bounded-error randomized algorithm decides 3-SAT on n variables in time 2^{δn}·poly(input size)), then
there is δ' > 0 such that no bounded-error randomized algorithm decides γ-GapSVP in the ℓ₂ norm on rank-n
integer lattices in time 2^{δ'n}·poly(input size) (2^{Ω(n)} hardness, which in particular rules out
2^{o(n)}-time algorithms). (The alternative "obstruction" target is a meta-statement about a proof technique
and is not a mathematical proposition; it is not formalized.)
Formalization notes:
* Machine model: the board's canonical word-RAM block (pasted verbatim below): unit-cost word
  operations, word size w ≥ (wc+1)·log n with every input word fitting in a word, time O(T) means
  ⌊C·T + C⌋ steps, randomized = Monte Carlo with two-sided error 1/3 over a uniformly random tape
  (`WRRandSolvesIn`). Since an input integer must fit in one word, w is at least the bit length of the
  largest entry; this is the standard trans-dichotomous convention, and since a w-bit word operation is
  simulated in poly(w) ≤ poly(input bits) bit operations, it changes running times only by the poly(size)
  factor that every time bound below already allows.
* 3-SAT: `CNF3` has `n` variables and a list of clauses of at most 3 literals (variable, sign); encoded as
  `[n, #clauses]` followed by 3 words per clause (literal code 2(v+1)+sign, 0 = empty slot), an injective
  encoding. `RETH` := ∃ δ > 0, ∀ c, no randomized algorithm decides satisfiability in time
  O(2^{δn}·L^c), L = number of input words. This is randomized ETH (Dell–Husfeldt–Marx–Taslaman–Wahlén);
  the poly(L) factor is harmless (duplicates can be removed, so L ≤ poly(n)).
* GapSVP_γ (ℓ₂): instance = integer basis B ∈ ℤ^{d×n} (columns = basis vectors, rank n) and an integer
  threshold r for the SQUARED length. YES: columns linearly independent over ℚ and some nonzero integer
  combination v has ‖Bv‖² ≤ r. NO: columns independent and every nonzero v has ‖Bv‖² > γ²·r. Outside the
  promise any output is accepted (`Correct` is an implication). Rational bases reduce to integer ones by
  scaling, so integer bases are the standard form. Entries are encoded by `wrInt` (zig-zag); the size
  parameter is the total bit length `svpBits` of the encoding.
* Claim := ∃ γ > 1, RETH → ∃ δ > 0, ∀ c, ¬ WRRandSolvesIn (GapSVP γ) (2^{δn}·(bits+1)^c). Here n is the
  lattice rank. Proving Claim = the desired fine-grained reduction for p = 2 (what AGMZ prove for p > 2).
  ¬Claim would mean: for every γ > 1, rETH holds yet GapSVP_γ is solvable in time 2^{δn}poly for every
  δ > 0 — i.e. (since ¬(A→B) = A ∧ ¬B) a proof of rETH, so ¬Claim is not provable without resolving
  rETH; this is the usual status of conditional hardness statements.
* Loophole audit: the model has algorithms (brute force over bounded coefficient vectors solves GapSVP in
  2^{O(n log n)}·poly), so "no algorithm" is not vacuous; the promise sets are nonempty; γ is a fixed real
  > 1 chosen before the algorithm; δ and the constants C, c of the algorithm are quantified so that the
  conclusion is exactly 2^{Ω(n)}·poly hardness.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM027
noncomputable section

/-! ### Canonical word-RAM model (QED board, shared block; paste verbatim inside the problem namespace)

* A machine has word size `w`; every register and memory cell holds a natural number `< 2^w`
  (invariant: every register write is reduced mod `2^w`; memory only receives register values
  and input words, which are required to be `< 2^w`).
* Registers `R : ℕ → ℕ` (a program mentions only finitely many) and memory `M : ℕ → ℕ`
  (addresses are register values, hence `< 2^w`: at most `2^w` cells, all initially 0 except input).
* Program: a finite list of the standard unit-cost instructions below; `pc` indexes the list.
  A `pc` outside the list (in particular after `halt`, or a jump past the end) means halted, and a
  halted configuration is a fixed point of `wrStep`.
* Input: a list of words `x₀ … x_{n-1}` placed in `M[0..n-1]`; initially `R 0 = n`, `R 1 = w`,
  all other registers 0. Output: on halting, `M[0 .. R 0 - 1]`.
* Randomness: instruction `rand d` reads the next word of a random tape (word `k` is
  `tape k mod 2^w`). Deterministic runs use the all-zero tape.
* Cost: one step per instruction. `RunsWithin` asks the machine to be halted after `t` steps.
* Word size: an algorithm carries a constant `wc`, and must be correct for EVERY word size
  `w ≥ (wc+1)·(⌊log₂(n+1)⌋+1)` for which all input words fit (`< 2^w`). Requiring all such `w`
  (rather than letting the algorithm pick `w`) rules out the "huge word" loophole: the time bound
  must already hold at `w = Θ(log n)`, while larger `w` never hurts (the program can mask).
-/

/-- The instruction set (all unit cost). Indices `d a b` are register names, `t` a program address. -/
inductive WRInstr where
  /-- `R d := c mod 2^w` (a fixed program constant). -/
  | const (d c : ℕ)
  /-- `R d := M[R a]` (indirect load). -/
  | load (d a : ℕ)
  /-- `M[R a] := R s` (indirect store). -/
  | store (a s : ℕ)
  /-- `R d := (R a + R b) mod 2^w`. -/
  | add (d a b : ℕ)
  /-- `R d := R a - R b`, truncated at 0. -/
  | sub (d a b : ℕ)
  /-- `R d := (R a * R b) mod 2^w` (low word of the product). -/
  | mul (d a b : ℕ)
  /-- `R d := ⌊R a / R b⌋` (and `x / 0 = 0`). -/
  | div (d a b : ℕ)
  /-- Bitwise and / or / xor. -/
  | band (d a b : ℕ)
  | bor (d a b : ℕ)
  | bxor (d a b : ℕ)
  /-- `R d := (R a · 2^(R b)) mod 2^w` and `R d := ⌊R a / 2^(R b)⌋`. -/
  | shl (d a b : ℕ)
  | shr (d a b : ℕ)
  /-- Unconditional jump; jump if `R a = 0`; jump if `R a < R b`. -/
  | jmp (t : ℕ)
  | jz (a t : ℕ)
  | jlt (a b t : ℕ)
  /-- `R d :=` next random word. -/
  | rand (d : ℕ)
  /-- Stop. -/
  | halt

/-- Machine configuration: program counter, registers, memory, number of random words used. -/
structure WRCfg where
  pc : ℕ
  reg : ℕ → ℕ
  mem : ℕ → ℕ
  rc : ℕ

/-- One step of program `prog` with word size `w` and random tape `tape`. -/
def wrStep (prog : List WRInstr) (w : ℕ) (tape : ℕ → ℕ) (s : WRCfg) : WRCfg :=
  match prog[s.pc]? with
  | none => s
  | some ins =>
    let upd : ℕ → ℕ → WRCfg := fun d v =>
      { s with pc := s.pc + 1, reg := Function.update s.reg d (v % 2 ^ w) }
    let jump : Bool → ℕ → WRCfg := fun b t =>
      { s with pc := if b then t else s.pc + 1 }
    match ins with
    | .const d c => upd d c
    | .load d a => upd d (s.mem (s.reg a))
    | .store a r => { s with pc := s.pc + 1, mem := Function.update s.mem (s.reg a) (s.reg r) }
    | .add d a b => upd d (s.reg a + s.reg b)
    | .sub d a b => upd d (s.reg a - s.reg b)
    | .mul d a b => upd d (s.reg a * s.reg b)
    | .div d a b => upd d (s.reg a / s.reg b)
    | .band d a b => upd d (Nat.land (s.reg a) (s.reg b))
    | .bor d a b => upd d (Nat.lor (s.reg a) (s.reg b))
    | .bxor d a b => upd d (Nat.xor (s.reg a) (s.reg b))
    | .shl d a b => upd d (s.reg a * 2 ^ (s.reg b))
    | .shr d a b => upd d (s.reg a / 2 ^ (s.reg b))
    | .jmp t => { s with pc := t }
    | .jz a t => jump (decide (s.reg a = 0)) t
    | .jlt a b t => jump (decide (s.reg a < s.reg b)) t
    | .rand d =>
        { s with pc := s.pc + 1, reg := Function.update s.reg d (tape s.rc % 2 ^ w), rc := s.rc + 1 }
    | .halt => { s with pc := prog.length }

/-- Initial configuration: input in `M[0..n-1]`, `R 0 = n`, `R 1 = w`. -/
def wrInit (w : ℕ) (input : List ℕ) : WRCfg where
  pc := 0
  reg := fun i => if i = 0 then input.length else if i = 1 then w else 0
  mem := fun a => input.getD a 0
  rc := 0

/-- Output of a configuration: `M[0 .. R 0 - 1]`. -/
def wrOutput (s : WRCfg) : List ℕ := (List.range (s.reg 0)).map s.mem

/-- Halted: the program counter has left the program. -/
def WRHalted (prog : List WRInstr) (s : WRCfg) : Prop := prog.length ≤ s.pc

/-- With random tape `tape`, the run on `input` has halted after `t` steps (i.e. within `t` steps,
since halted configurations are fixed points) with output `out`. -/
def RunsWithinR (prog : List WRInstr) (w : ℕ) (tape : ℕ → ℕ) (input : List ℕ) (t : ℕ)
    (out : List ℕ) : Prop :=
  WRHalted prog ((wrStep prog w tape)^[t] (wrInit w input)) ∧
    wrOutput ((wrStep prog w tape)^[t] (wrInit w input)) = out

/-- Deterministic run (all-zero random tape). -/
def RunsWithin (prog : List WRInstr) (w : ℕ) (input : List ℕ) (t : ℕ) (out : List ℕ) : Prop :=
  RunsWithinR prog w (fun _ => 0) input t out

/-- An algorithm: a program and a word-size constant `wc` (it may assume `w ≥ (wc+1)·log n`). -/
structure WRAlgo where
  prog : List WRInstr
  wc : ℕ

/-- Admissible word sizes for an input: `w ≥ (wc+1)(⌊log₂(n+1)⌋+1)` (so `n < 2^w`) and every
input word fits in `w` bits. -/
def WROK (wc : ℕ) (input : List ℕ) (w : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (wc + 1) * (Nat.log 2 (input.length + 1) + 1) ≤ w ∧ ∀ x ∈ input, x < 2 ^ w

/-- The step budget `⌊C·T + C⌋₊` used for "time O(T)" (the additive `C` absorbs small inputs). -/
def wrBudget (C T : ℝ) : ℕ := ⌊C * T + C⌋₊

/-- A (batch) problem: instances, a word encoding of each instance, and the set of correct outputs. -/
structure WRProblem where
  Inst : Type
  enc : Inst → List ℕ
  Correct : Inst → List ℕ → Prop

/-- Deterministic: some algorithm solves every instance `x` within `O(T x)` steps, for every
admissible word size. (`T` may depend on any parameters of the instance.) -/
def WRSolvesIn (P : WRProblem) (T : P.Inst → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ A : WRAlgo, ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x : P.Inst, ∀ w : ℕ, WROK A.wc (P.enc x) w →
    ∃ out : List ℕ, RunsWithin A.prog w (P.enc x) (wrBudget C (T x)) out ∧ P.Correct x out

/-- The random tape determined by `L` random `w`-bit words (word `k ≥ L` reads as 0; a run of `L`
steps reads at most `L` words, so uniform `f` is exactly a uniformly random tape). -/
def wrTape {L w : ℕ} (f : Fin L → Fin (2 ^ w)) : ℕ → ℕ :=
  fun k => if h : k < L then (f ⟨k, h⟩ : ℕ) else 0

/-- Randomized (Monte Carlo, worst-case time): for every instance and admissible `w`, at least 2/3
of the random tapes make the algorithm halt within `O(T x)` steps with a correct output. -/
def WRRandSolvesIn (P : WRProblem) (T : P.Inst → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ A : WRAlgo, ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x : P.Inst, ∀ w : ℕ, WROK A.wc (P.enc x) w →
    2 * (2 ^ w) ^ (wrBudget C (T x)) ≤
      3 * Nat.card {f : Fin (wrBudget C (T x)) → Fin (2 ^ w) //
        ∃ out : List ℕ, RunsWithinR A.prog w (wrTape f) (P.enc x) (wrBudget C (T x)) out ∧
          P.Correct x out}

/-! #### Online (multi-phase) variant
Phase inputs `x₀, x₁, …` arrive one at a time. Before phase `j` the words of `x_j` overwrite
`M[0..|x_j|-1]`, `R 0 := |x_j|`, `pc := 0`; all other registers, memory and the random-tape position
persist. The phase's output is read when it halts. Phase `j` cannot see `x_{j+1}`, so answers are
online. Inputs are fixed in advance (oblivious adversary). -/

/-- Feed the next phase input into a (halted) configuration. -/
def wrFeed (s : WRCfg) (x : List ℕ) : WRCfg :=
  { s with pc := 0, reg := Function.update s.reg 0 x.length,
           mem := fun a => if a < x.length then x.getD a 0 else s.mem a }

/-- `wrPhases prog w tape s xs ts os`: starting from `s`, phase `j` gets input `xs[j]`, halts within
`ts[j]` steps and outputs `os[j]`. -/
def wrPhases (prog : List WRInstr) (w : ℕ) (tape : ℕ → ℕ) :
    WRCfg → List (List ℕ) → List ℕ → List (List ℕ) → Prop
  | _, [], [], [] => True
  | s, x :: xs, t :: ts, o :: os =>
      WRHalted prog ((wrStep prog w tape)^[t] (wrFeed s x)) ∧
      wrOutput ((wrStep prog w tape)^[t] (wrFeed s x)) = o ∧
      wrPhases prog w tape ((wrStep prog w tape)^[t] (wrFeed s x)) xs ts os
  | _, _, _, _ => False

/-- An online problem: instances, the list of phase inputs, and correct lists of phase outputs. -/
structure WROnlineProblem where
  Inst : Type
  phases : Inst → List (List ℕ)
  Correct : Inst → List (List ℕ) → Prop

/-- All words of all phases. -/
def wrAllWords (xs : List (List ℕ)) : List ℕ := xs.foldr (· ++ ·) []

/-- Randomized online solution with first-phase (preprocessing) time `O(Tpre x)` and total time of
all later phases `O(Tq x)` (so amortized time per later phase is `Tq x / (#phases - 1)`). -/
def WROnlineRandSolvesIn (P : WROnlineProblem) (Tpre Tq : P.Inst → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ A : WRAlgo, ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x : P.Inst, ∀ w : ℕ, WROK A.wc (wrAllWords (P.phases x)) w →
    2 * (2 ^ w) ^ (wrBudget C (Tpre x) + wrBudget C (Tq x)) ≤
      3 * Nat.card {f : Fin (wrBudget C (Tpre x) + wrBudget C (Tq x)) → Fin (2 ^ w) //
        ∃ ts : List ℕ, ∃ outs : List (List ℕ),
          wrPhases A.prog w (wrTape f) (wrInit w []) (P.phases x) ts outs ∧
          (ts.take 1).sum ≤ wrBudget C (Tpre x) ∧ (ts.drop 1).sum ≤ wrBudget C (Tq x) ∧
          P.Correct x outs}

/-- Deterministic online solution (all-zero tape). -/
def WROnlineSolvesIn (P : WROnlineProblem) (Tpre Tq : P.Inst → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ A : WRAlgo, ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x : P.Inst, ∀ w : ℕ, WROK A.wc (wrAllWords (P.phases x)) w →
    ∃ ts : List ℕ, ∃ outs : List (List ℕ),
      wrPhases A.prog w (fun _ => 0) (wrInit w []) (P.phases x) ts outs ∧
      (ts.take 1).sum ≤ wrBudget C (Tpre x) ∧ (ts.drop 1).sum ≤ wrBudget C (Tq x) ∧
      P.Correct x outs

/-! #### Encoding helpers -/

/-- Boolean as a word. -/
def wrBit (b : Bool) : ℕ := cond b 1 0

/-- Integer as a word (zig-zag: `z ≥ 0 ↦ 2z`, `z < 0 ↦ 2|z| + 1`). -/
def wrInt (z : ℤ) : ℕ := 2 * z.natAbs + (if z < 0 then 1 else 0)

/-- A list of pairs as a flat list of words. -/
def wrPairs : List (ℕ × ℕ) → List ℕ
  | [] => []
  | p :: l => p.1 :: p.2 :: wrPairs l

/-- Output `out` is the yes/no answer to `b`: `[1]` if `b`, `[0]` otherwise. -/
def WRAnswer (b : Prop) (out : List ℕ) : Prop := (b ∧ out = [1]) ∨ (¬ b ∧ out = [0])

/-! ### 3-SAT and randomized ETH -/

/-- A 3-CNF formula on `n` variables: each clause is a list of at most 3 literals (variable, sign). -/
structure CNF3 where
  n : ℕ
  clauses : List (List (Fin n × Bool))
  short : ∀ cl ∈ clauses, cl.length ≤ 3

/-- `σ` satisfies `φ`: every clause has a literal `(v, b)` with `σ v = b`. -/
def CNF3.Sat (φ : CNF3) : Prop :=
  ∃ σ : Fin φ.n → Bool, ∀ cl ∈ φ.clauses, ∃ l ∈ cl, σ l.1 = l.2

/-- Literal code `2(v+1) + sign` (never 0). -/
def litCode {n : ℕ} (l : Fin n × Bool) : ℕ := 2 * ((l.1 : ℕ) + 1) + wrBit l.2

/-- A clause as exactly 3 words (padded with 0). -/
def clauseCode {n : ℕ} (cl : List (Fin n × Bool)) : List ℕ :=
  (cl.map litCode ++ [0, 0, 0]).take 3

/-- Word encoding of a formula. -/
def CNF3.enc (φ : CNF3) : List ℕ :=
  [φ.n, φ.clauses.length] ++ wrAllWords (φ.clauses.map clauseCode)

/-- The decision problem 3-SAT. -/
def SAT3 : WRProblem where
  Inst := CNF3
  enc := CNF3.enc
  Correct := fun (φ : CNF3) (out : List ℕ) => WRAnswer φ.Sat out

/-- Randomized ETH: for some `δ > 0` no bounded-error randomized algorithm decides 3-SAT in time
`O(2^{δ n} · L^c)` (`L` = number of input words), for any `c`. -/
def RETH : Prop :=
  ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ c : ℕ,
    ¬ WRRandSolvesIn SAT3 (fun φ : CNF3 => (2 : ℝ) ^ (δ * (φ.n : ℝ)) * ((φ.enc.length : ℝ)) ^ c)

/-! ### GapSVP in the ℓ₂ norm -/

/-- An SVP instance: basis matrix `B` (`d × n`, columns are the basis vectors) and a threshold `r` for
the squared length. -/
structure SVPInst where
  d : ℕ
  n : ℕ
  B : Fin d → Fin n → ℤ
  r : ℕ

/-- `‖B v‖₂²` for an integer coefficient vector `v`. -/
def SVPInst.normSq (x : SVPInst) (v : Fin x.n → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  ∑ i : Fin x.d, (∑ j : Fin x.n, x.B i j * v j) ^ 2

/-- The columns of `B` are linearly independent (so the lattice has rank `n`). -/
def SVPInst.Indep (x : SVPInst) : Prop :=
  LinearIndependent ℚ (fun j : Fin x.n => fun i : Fin x.d => ((x.B i j : ℤ) : ℚ))

/-- YES instances: `λ₁(L(B))² ≤ r`. -/
def SVPInst.Yes (x : SVPInst) : Prop :=
  x.Indep ∧ ∃ v : Fin x.n → ℤ, v ≠ 0 ∧ x.normSq v ≤ (x.r : ℤ)

/-- NO instances: `λ₁(L(B))² > γ² r`. -/
def SVPInst.No (γ : ℝ) (x : SVPInst) : Prop :=
  x.Indep ∧ ∀ v : Fin x.n → ℤ, v ≠ 0 → γ ^ 2 * (x.r : ℝ) < ((x.normSq v : ℤ) : ℝ)

/-- Encoding `[d, n, r]` followed by the entries of `B` row-major (zig-zag integers). -/
def SVPInst.enc (x : SVPInst) : List ℕ :=
  [x.d, x.n, x.r] ++
    List.ofFn (fun t : Fin (x.d * x.n) =>
      wrInt (x.B (finProdFinEquiv.symm t).1 (finProdFinEquiv.symm t).2))

/-- Total bit length of the encoding. -/
def SVPInst.bits (x : SVPInst) : ℕ := (x.enc.map (fun a : ℕ => Nat.log 2 a + 1)).sum

/-- The promise problem `γ`-GapSVP (ℓ₂): output `[1]` on YES, `[0]` on NO, anything otherwise. -/
def GapSVP (γ : ℝ) : WRProblem where
  Inst := SVPInst
  enc := SVPInst.enc
  Correct := fun (x : SVPInst) (out : List ℕ) => (x.Yes → out = [1]) ∧ (x.No γ → out = [0])

/-- Some `γ > 1` is such that randomized ETH implies `2^{Ω(n)}` (times any polynomial in the input
size) randomized hardness of `γ`-GapSVP in the ℓ₂ norm on rank-`n` lattices. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ γ : ℝ, 1 < γ ∧
    (RETH → ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ c : ℕ,
      ¬ WRRandSolvesIn (GapSVP γ)
          (fun x : SVPInst => (2 : ℝ) ^ (δ * (x.n : ℝ)) * ((x.bits : ℝ) + 1) ^ c))

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM027

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M028: A super-constant-degree SoS integrality gap for Unique Games
Construct Unique Games instances of optimum value at most ε on which the degree-d Sum-of-Squares
relaxation still has value at least 1 - ε, with alphabet size depending only on ε and degree d
growing without bound; the alternative is that constant-degree SoS distinguishes (1-ε)-satisfiable
from δ-satisfiable instances for every alphabet size.
Informal statement: (Gap) For every ε > 0 there is q = q(ε) such that for every degree bound D there is
a Unique Games instance over alphabet [q] with optimum ≤ ε on which the degree-2D SoS (Lasserre)
relaxation has value ≥ 1 - ε (equivalently: a family of instances of growing size n with
degree d(n) = ω(1) gaps). The (Algorithm) alternative in the original statement is exactly the
negation of (Gap), so the original disjunction was a tautology; Claim is (Gap) alone.
Formalization notes: A `UGInstance q` has `n` variables, `m` constraints, the e-th constraint asks
`perm e (f (src e)) = f (dst e)`. `value f` is the satisfied fraction. The SoS relaxation of degree 2D
uses Boolean variables `X (v,i)` ("v gets label i") and a pseudo-expectation: an ℝ-linear functional
`L` on `MvPolynomial (Fin n × Fin q) ℝ` with `L 1 = 1`, `L (p*p) ≥ 0` for `deg p ≤ D`, and
`L (p * g) = 0` for each constraint polynomial `g` (`X^2 - X`, `∑_i X (v,i) - 1`) whenever
`deg p + deg g ≤ 2D`. The SoS value is the sup of `L objective`; "value ≥ 1 - ε" is encoded by
existence of such an `L` (the sup is attained by compactness, so this is equivalent).
Proving `Claim` = constructing the super-constant-degree gap (strong evidence for UGC-type hardness of SoS).
Proving `¬Claim` = there are ε, δ (take δ = ε) such that for every q some constant degree D refutes
all instances of value ≤ ε, i.e. the algorithmic side (which would refute UGC unless P = NP).
Note: for fixed instance size, degree ≥ n·q SoS is exact, so the instances must grow with D.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM028

/-- A Unique Games instance over alphabet `Fin q`: `n` variables, `m` permutation constraints. -/
structure UGInstance (q : ℕ) where
  n : ℕ
  m : ℕ
  src : Fin m → Fin n
  dst : Fin m → Fin n
  perm : Fin m → Equiv.Perm (Fin q)

/-- Fraction of constraints satisfied by the labelling `f`. -/
noncomputable def UGInstance.value {q : ℕ} (I : UGInstance q) (f : Fin I.n → Fin q) : ℝ :=
  ((Finset.univ.filter (fun e : Fin I.m => I.perm e (f (I.src e)) = f (I.dst e))).card : ℝ) /
    (I.m : ℝ)

/-- The degree-2 objective polynomial: average over constraints of `∑_i x_{src,i} x_{dst,π i}`. -/
noncomputable def UGInstance.objective {q : ℕ} (I : UGInstance q) :
    MvPolynomial (Fin I.n × Fin q) ℝ :=
  MvPolynomial.C ((I.m : ℝ)⁻¹) *
    ∑ e : Fin I.m, ∑ i : Fin q,
      MvPolynomial.X (I.src e, i) * MvPolynomial.X (I.dst e, I.perm e i)

/-- `L` is a degree-`2D` SoS pseudo-expectation for the Boolean one-hot encoding of `I`. -/
def IsPseudoExpectation {q : ℕ} (I : UGInstance q) (D : ℕ)
    (L : MvPolynomial (Fin I.n × Fin q) ℝ →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ) : Prop :=
  L 1 = 1 ∧
  (∀ p : MvPolynomial (Fin I.n × Fin q) ℝ, p.totalDegree ≤ D → 0 ≤ L (p * p)) ∧
  (∀ (p : MvPolynomial (Fin I.n × Fin q) ℝ) (v : Fin I.n) (i : Fin q),
      p.totalDegree + 2 ≤ 2 * D →
      L (p * (MvPolynomial.X (v, i) * MvPolynomial.X (v, i) - MvPolynomial.X (v, i))) = 0) ∧
  (∀ (p : MvPolynomial (Fin I.n × Fin q) ℝ) (v : Fin I.n),
      p.totalDegree + 1 ≤ 2 * D →
      L (p * ((∑ i : Fin q, MvPolynomial.X (v, i)) - 1)) = 0)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ q : ℕ, ∀ D : ℕ, ∃ I : UGInstance q,
    0 < I.m ∧
    (∀ f : Fin I.n → Fin q, I.value f ≤ ε) ∧
    ∃ L : MvPolynomial (Fin I.n × Fin q) ℝ →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ,
      IsPseudoExpectation I D L ∧ 1 - ε ≤ L I.objective

end OpenProblems.QEDM028
